context: 1. “Nuclear weapons were never Ukrainian” — Partially true. Yes, the nuclear weapons located on Ukrainian territory after the collapse of the USSR were part of the Soviet strategic arsenal, and the control codes were indeed in Moscow. Ukraine did not have direct access to those codes. — However, this does not mean Ukraine couldn’t theoretically gain control over these weapons. There were experts and infrastructure capable of working with the delivery systems. 2. The “Kazakhstan and Baikonur” analogy — This is a false analogy. Kazakhstan did not have its own production base for space technology. — In contrast, Ukraine had a very powerful rocket and space industry — the Yuzhnoye Design Bureau and Yuzhmash plant developed and produced intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), such as the R-36 “Satan”. Ukraine played a crucial role in Soviet missile development. 3. “Ukraine scrapped its Tu-160 fleet” — This is true, but with context. Yes, some Tu-160 bombers were destroyed under agreements with the US as part of the Nunn-Lugar program (with American financial support). — However, some Tu-160s were transferred to Russia as part of a debt repayment deal (in 1999). — Ukraine simply could not afford to maintain such expensive aircraft in the midst of the severe economic crisis of the 1990s. 4. “Where is Ukraine’s ICBM or aerospace industry today?” — This is manipulation. Ukraine’s aerospace industry still exists, although it suffered heavily after 2014 due to the breakdown of cooperation with Russia. — Yuzhnoye and Yuzhmash are still operational, albeit at reduced capacity. Ukraine has also been actively involved in international space projects, such as building the first stage of the Antares rocket for the US.
